explanations.explanation: Paul says it plainly: “…how dare he go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints!” He wants the grievance kept among believers. Think of it as settling things at your own kitchen table before calling in a stranger to referee.

I can see why that one tempts you, but priests never come up in this passage. Paul says the believer should go before “the saints,” not before the unrighteous. So the answer is the saints, friend. Nobody in a fancy robe is needed.

No governor anywhere in these verses. Paul says a believer shouldn't go to law before the unrighteous and should go before the saints instead. A governor with a big chair isn't who he has in mind. He's pointing at the church family.

That's right, and Paul asks it like it's obvious: “Do you not know that the saints will judge the world?” He's reminding the Corinthians how big their calling is. I'd say that's the kind of question that makes you sit up straight at the table.

Paul actually says the opposite of False here. He asks, “Do you not know that the saints will judge the world?” He says it to remind the Corinthians what is ahead for them. So this one is True, friend.

Yes, trivial. Paul asks, “And if you are to judge the world, are you not competent to judge trivial cases?” His point is that if they can handle the big job, the small stuff should be no trouble. It's like being trusted with the whole kitchen and then panicking over a crooked cookie.

Paul doesn't say anything about ancient cases. His word is “trivial,” as in small everyday disputes. He's setting the world-sized job next to the little stuff. So the little cases are the ones he says they can handle.
Foreign cases never come up here. Paul asks if they aren't “competent to judge trivial cases?” The comparison is big job against small job, not home against far away. Small is the word he wants.

Angels it is. Paul asks, “Do you not know that we will judge angels?” Then he adds, “How much more the things of this life!” If you'll be doing that, a squabble over everyday stuff is small potatoes, friend.

Prophets aren't named in these verses. After saying the saints will judge the world, Paul goes bigger with, “Do you not know that we will judge angels?” Angels are the answer. And that's a long way up from a dispute over everyday matters.
Paul never mentions kings of Israel here. He says, “Do you not know that we will judge angels?” That's even bigger than the world. Then he finishes with, “How much more the things of this life!”

explanations.answer: Someone wise enough to settle it between brothers
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Paul asks, “Is there really no one among you wise enough to arbitrate between his brothers?” He says it to their shame. I think he's hoping somebody in that church stands up and says, “I'll help.”

explanations.answer: Enough money to pay the court fees
explanations.explanation: Money never comes up in these verses. Paul asks, “Is there really no one among you wise enough to arbitrate between his brothers?” What he's asking about is wisdom. He isn't asking about a wallet.

explanations.answer: A building big enough to hold trials
explanations.explanation: Paul says nothing about buildings or room sizes. What he asks is, “Is there really no one among you wise enough to arbitrate between his brothers?” The missing thing he names is a wise person among them. A bigger room wouldn't fix that, friend.

Unbelievers, yes. Paul says, “Instead, one brother goes to law against another, and this in front of unbelievers!” So the dispute is out in the open for people outside the church to watch. That's the part that gets him going.
Apostles aren't who Paul has in mind here. He says the brother goes to law against another “in front of unbelievers!” That's the sting. The audience is people who don't believe.
Prophets don't show up in this verse. Paul says it happens “in front of unbelievers!” The word he uses for the audience is unbelievers. He's not talking about prophets at all, friend.

Right. Paul says, “The very fact that you have lawsuits among you means that you are thoroughly defeated already.” It's about having the lawsuits at all, before anyone even wins. Having a winner doesn't change that.

Paul says the opposite of False here. His words are, “The very fact that you have lawsuits among you means that you are thoroughly defeated already.” So just having them counts as a loss. That makes this one True, friend.

Yes, that's the hard one. Paul asks, “Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated?” It's tough to hear. Honestly, I'd rather take on a whole batch of dough by hand than swallow that, but that's the question he asks.

explanations.answer: Take it to a higher court
explanations.explanation: A higher court isn't what Paul suggests. He's asking why they go to law at all, and he says, “Why not rather be wronged?” The hard thing he names is letting themselves be wronged. He doesn't point to another court, friend.

explanations.answer: Ask Paul to come and decide
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't offer to come and decide anything here. His question is, “Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated?” The hard thing he names is being willing to be wronged. Nobody gets called in as a judge.

explanations.answer: Cheating and wronging their own brothers
explanations.explanation: That's what Paul says. “Instead, you yourselves cheat and do wrong, even against your own brothers!” They were asked why they wouldn't take being wronged, and they were the ones doing it. I think that line hits close to home.

explanations.answer: Forgiving and forgetting way too fast
explanations.explanation: Paul says nothing like that here. He says, “Instead, you yourselves cheat and do wrong, even against your own brothers!” So the trouble is the cheating and wronging, not too much forgiving. Nobody is accused of being too quick to let things go.

explanations.answer: Keeping quiet and staying far away
explanations.explanation: Quiet and distant isn't the picture Paul paints. He says, “Instead, you yourselves cheat and do wrong, even against your own brothers!” They were up close and doing it. So the answer is the cheating and wronging.

Paul says the opposite. His question is, “Do you not know that the wicked will not inherit the kingdom of God?” Then he adds, “Do not be deceived.” So the answer is False, and he doesn't want anyone fooled about it.
That's right. Paul asks, “Do you not know that the wicked will not inherit the kingdom of God?” Then he warns, “Do not be deceived.” He wants the Corinthians to see it clearly.
Yes. After the list he says, “And that is what some of you were.” Notice the word were. It tells us where they started and sets up what comes next. That's good news waiting right around the corner.

Paul actually says it about them. Right after his list he writes, “And that is what some of you were.” So some of the Corinthians really did have that past. But he doesn't stop there, friend, and the next words matter.

explanations.answer: They were washed and made holy and right with God
explanations.explanation: That's it. Paul says, “But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified…” That's three big words, all pointing to what was done for them. It's one of my favorite turns in the whole letter.

explanations.answer: They still have to earn their way back to God
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say anything about earning. He says, “But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified…” Those words say what was already done for them. The “But” tells you the past isn't the end of the story.

explanations.answer: They are no different from how they used to be
explanations.explanation: Paul says the opposite. He writes, “But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified…” That's a real change, friend. The little word “But” carries a lot of weight here.

Right. Paul says it was “in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.” Both are named together there. When I think of the day someone reached into my drawer and called me out, I get a little misty myself.

The apostles in Jerusalem aren't named in this verse. Paul says they were washed “in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.” So it's the Spirit of our God who's named. No other group is mentioned.
Elders aren't mentioned in these verses. Paul says it happened “in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.” That's who he names, friend. He doesn't name any church leaders.
